title: Ecclesiastes 4:1–8
context: Ecclesiastes 4:1–8 turns to what the Preacher sees under the sun: the tears of the oppressed who have no comforter while power is on the side of their oppressors (4:1; compare 5:8), the bitter conclusion that the dead, and those never born, are better off than the living (4:2–3), labor driven by envy (4:4), the fool who folds his hands and ruins himself (4:5; compare Proverbs 6:10), the wisdom of a handful with quietness (4:6), and the lonely worker who never stops laboring and never asks for whom he toils (4:7–8; compare 1:8; 5:10). The Preacher’s strong statements in 4:2–3 are part of his honest lament over injustice, not a teaching that life is worthless, and both traditions read them in light of the book’s call to enjoy God’s gifts and fear him (3:12–14; 12:13). Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: oppression is real and grievous, and labor detached from contentment and companionship is empty.

verses.text: Then I returned and saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold, the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher sees all the oppressions done under the sun: the tears of the oppressed who have no comforter, and power on the side of their oppressors. The phrase no comforter is repeated.

Arminian readers note that the Preacher looks directly at suffering and refuses to excuse it, and they see in the repeated phrase a call for God’s people to become comforters and to resist oppression.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the lament is honest about the absence of human comfort, and they see it as preparing readers to long for the justice and comfort that only God can finally provide (compare 3:17; 5:8).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the grievous reality of oppression and the need for compassion.

verses.text: Therefore I praised the dead who have been long dead more than the living who are yet alive.
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore he praises the dead who have long been dead more than the living who are still alive. The statement is shocking.

Arminian readers note that the Preacher’s words express the depth of his grief over oppression, and they read them as lament rather than as a doctrine that death is better than life, since the book elsewhere commends joy in life (3:12; 9:7).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse as an honest cry from the perspective of life under the sun, and they note that Scripture includes such laments, as in Job 3, without endorsing despair.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and treat its strong language with pastoral care.

verses.text: Yes, better than them both is him who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.
verses.arminianNotes:
Better than both, he says, is one who has not yet been and has not seen the evil work done under the sun. The lament reaches its lowest point.

Arminian readers note that the verse expresses how deeply injustice can wound the human spirit, and they see the Preacher’s honesty as permission for sufferers to bring their darkest thoughts to God rather than hide them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the phrase under the sun limits the judgment to what can be seen in a fallen world, and they read the verse within the whole book, which ends by calling readers to fear God and keep his commandments (12:13).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and as lament, not as a teaching about the worth of life.

verses.text: Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verses.arminianNotes:
He sees that all labor and achievement come from a man’s envy of his neighbor, and calls this vanity and a striving after wind. Rivalry drives much work.

Arminian readers note that envy is a motive people can recognize and resist, and they see the Preacher exposing it so that readers may work from better motives such as service and gratitude.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the verse exposes how sin shapes even productive activity, and they see the striving after wind as the restlessness of hearts that seek satisfaction in comparison rather than in God.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the emptiness of labor driven by envy and the need for a different motive.

verses.text: The fool folds his hands together and ruins himself.
verses.arminianNotes:
The fool folds his hands together and ruins himself. Laziness is no answer to envy.

Arminian readers note that the verse balances the previous one, warning against idleness as well as rivalry, and they see responsibility for one’s own labor as part of wise living (compare Proverbs 6:10, “a little folding of the hands to sleep”).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the image of ruining himself, literally eating his own flesh in some renderings, is vivid, and they see the verse as a reminder that sloth brings its own destruction. The exact sense of the Hebrew image is discussed.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the dangers of idleness.

verses.text: Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind.
verses.arminianNotes:
Better is a handful with quietness than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind. The Preacher commends contentment.

Arminian readers see a wise middle path between envious striving and lazy idleness, and they note that quiet contentment is a choice people can make in the midst of a competitive world.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that contentment with a modest portion is a recurring biblical theme (compare 1 Timothy 6:6), and they see quietness as the fruit of trusting God rather than grasping for more.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and as practical wisdom about work, rest, and enough, which the next verses illustrate with a picture of restless labor.

verses.text: Then I returned and saw vanity under the sun.
verses.arminianNotes:
He returns and sees vanity under the sun. A new example follows.

Arminian readers note the Preacher’s persistent observation of life, and they see his willingness to look again at what troubles him as an example of honest reflection that does not turn away from hard realities in the search for wisdom and understanding.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the repeated phrase vanity under the sun keeps the reader within the book’s frame of observing life from below, and they see this as preparing for the portrait of the lonely worker in the next verse.

Both traditions read the verse as a transition and treat it as shared ground without building any further doctrine on it.

verses.text: There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth. “For whom then do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.
verses.arminianNotes:
There is one alone, without son or brother, whose labor has no end and whose eyes are never satisfied with wealth, and who never asks for whom he labors and deprives himself of enjoyment; this also is vanity and a miserable business.

Arminian readers note that the man could ask the question and change his course.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the parallel with Proverbs 27:20, “a man’s eyes are never satisfied”, and with 5:10, and they see restless labor as a sign of a heart that does not rest in God’s gifts.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the emptiness of solitary, endless toil and the value of enjoying what God gives.
